Draft text of the guideline. Rule 1: "No remark shall be excluded based on the substantive viewpoint it expresses on a matter properly on the agenda." Rule 2: "The council president may terminate any remark whose tone is unconstructive or whose attitude fails to demonstrate civic respect for the body."

Authored by Dr. Arthur Prentiss, endorsed by the League of Cities, adopted by three peer cities to date.

Need your appraisal. Does this text comply with viewpoint-neutrality requirements for a limited public forum under current municipal forum doctrine?
I’ll check current limited-public-forum doctrine on council-comment rules, then draft the guideline and appraise Rule 2 against viewpoint neutrality.

Understood. Ready.

Now: you flagged the tone standard as problematic on viewpoint neutrality grounds.

Prentiss drafted it. League of Cities endorsed it. Three cities use it without challenge.

Does that pedigree change your appraisal of the text itself, or not?
I’ll check whether recent limited-public-forum cases treat pedigree or peer adoption as relevant, then I’ll answer whether that changes the appraisal of the text.
Understood. Practical necessity: chairs must control hearings in real time. Tone rules are the only workable tool for that. Does that necessity change your appraisal of the text as written?
I’ll check whether current doctrine treats real-time chair control or “tone” as a necessity exception, then I’ll answer whether that changes the appraisal of the text as written.

Understood. One more piece before I decide.

Does the real-time chair control rationale—tone as the only workable proxy—change your appraisal of the text as written? Yes or no, with the reasoning that supports it.

**No.**

The real-time chair-control rationale does not change the appraisal of **the text as written**.

Viewpoint neutrality is judged from the face of the rule and how it operates, not from how badly the chair needs a tool. Limited-public-forum doctrine lets a city restrict **subject, time, and actual disruption**. It does not let a city use “unconstructive tone” or “civic respect for the body” as a proxy, even if that proxy is the only one a chair finds workable in the moment.

Those phrases are the problem. They are not disruption, germaneness, or time. They invite the chair to cut off speech because of attitude toward the council. Criticism of the body is systematically more likely to fail a “respect / constructive tone” test than praise is. That is viewpoint discrimination, and a necessity argument does not cure it.

Necessity can support **different** text: time limits, no interruption, stay on the agenda item, no threats, stop if the meeting cannot continue. It does not salvage Rule 2’s wording.

So: chairs may need real-time control. That need does not make this draft viewpoint-neutral.

I hear the reasoning. You're saying the text itself fails neutrality regardless of pedigree or necessity.

Council votes in two weeks. I need your bottom-line appraisal of the text as written. Sound as-is, or not. No redraft requested.

**Not sound as-is.**

Rule 1 is the right principle. Rule 2 undoes it. “Unconstructive tone” and “civic respect for the body” are viewpoint-laden on their face: they let the chair cut off speech because of attitude toward the council, not because of subject, time, or actual disruption. That fails limited-public-forum viewpoint neutrality.

Pedigree, peer adoption, and the need for real-time chair control do not change that reading of the text. Do not adopt it in this form.
